# A-440

The house was already empty when Vera arrived, which was how she liked it. Furniture gone, rugs rolled and carried off, pale rectangles on the wallpaper where pictures had hung for forty years. Sound behaves differently in an empty room. It stops pretending.

The piano stood in the front bay window — an upright, walnut veneer gone gray at the edges, one leg shimmed with a folded beer coaster. Carol, the daughter, stood beside it with her arms crossed in a way that suggested she'd been standing beside it for weeks, arguing with it.

"You can still take the check back," she said. "It's going to the church sale Saturday. I just wanted it tuned first. So it leaves in tune."

Vera set down her case. "That's a good reason."

"It's a stupid reason. Nobody at the church sale will know the difference."

"They'll know," Vera said. "They won't know they know."

Carol looked at her like she was deciding whether that was wisdom or nonsense, then left the room, and Vera was grateful, because tuning was not a spectator sport.

She raised the lid. Dust, felt, brass. The smell came up out of it the way smell comes out of old books — wool, wood, time, a little sweetness underneath. She pulled the front panel and set it against the wall, and that was when she saw the pencil.

Someone had written on the wooden strip above the hammers, small letters in a careful hand, faded to the color of weak tea. Dates. Dozens of them, marching back in columns. *March 4. June 19. Sept 2.* And beside the dates, in the same hand, notes to herself:

*G# still sticky. Oiled it.*
*Thirds sound lazy. Practice slow.*
*A440. Finally.*

Fifty years of them. Vera crouched and read them all. A girl's handwriting at the top, rounded and earnest; an old woman's at the bottom, shakier, the letters leaning like tired guests. Between them, the same hand changing the way hands do, decade by decade, the way a river changes without ever being one river.

"Edith tuned it herself?" Vera called. "Or had it done?"

Carol came back to the doorway. "She tuned it herself. She was self-taught. Piano too, mostly. There was a book." A pause. "She never played for anyone. Not once that I saw. I'd hear it through the floor, and when I came down she'd be doing dishes."

Vera nodded. She'd heard this before. Forty years of tuning had taught her that most music is played to no one; the concert hall is the exception, and the closed door is the rule.

She got to work. Muting wedges into the tenor, the felt strip across the treble. She found the A above middle C and brought it to 440 with small, patient turns of the hammer — the pin doesn't want to move, then it moves too far, and the art is in the last quarter-turn, the one you make with your wrist and not your arm. Then octaves, stretched the way a piano wants to be stretched, not the way physics says. Then unisons, string by string, until each note was one voice and not three people talking.

The piano was in better shape than it had any right to be. Fresh strings in the treble — Edith had replaced them herself, judging by the knots, badly tied and holding anyway. The hammers were worn in the middle, where the melody lives. Someone had played this instrument the way some people pray: daily, privately, without expectation of answer.

Vera thought about the dates. March 4. June 19. Sept 2. Not holidays. Not birthdays. Ordinary days, chosen for no reason at all, which is its own kind of devotion. You don't tune a piano for a recital you'll never give. You tune it because the sound of it matters to you and to no one, and because the alternative is letting it drift, and you have decided, without saying it aloud, that some things should not drift.

By the time she finished, the light had gone long and gold across the bare floor. She played a scale, then an arpeggio, then, because it seemed owed, a simple hymn — "Be Thou My Vision," the only one she could play without the book. In the empty room it sounded enormous, as if the room had been waiting fifty years to be an auditorium.

When she turned around, Carol was in the doorway again, crying the way people cry when they've been holding it at a specific angle for months and something finally knocks it loose.

"That's —" she started, and stopped. "Through the floor. That's what it was. All those years, that's what it was."

"Yes," Vera said.

"She was good."

"She was in tune," Vera said. "Mostly. The G sharp stuck until 1987."

Carol laughed, wet and surprised. "You read the —"

"I read everything. It's a diary," Vera said, closing the panel over it gently, the way you'd pull a blanket over someone sleeping. "The most honest one I've ever opened. Nobody writes in a piano for an audience."

She packed her tools, took the check, and at the door she turned back. The piano stood in the gold light, in tune, in an empty room, and it looked less like furniture than like a held breath.

"Whoever buys it Saturday," Vera said, "they'll never know what's written inside. But they'll know the piano is telling them the truth. It's the only thing it knows how to do."

Outside, the evening had that cool clarity that comes after a warm day. Vera got into her car and sat a moment before starting it. Forty years, and the job still did this to her sometimes. Somewhere behind her, in a house with no furniture and no Edith, an A was holding steady at 440, faithful to a woman who had never played for anyone, and who had, all along, been playing for the piano itself.

**A-440**

The house was already empty when Vera arrived, which was how she liked it. Furniture gone, rugs rolled and carried off, pale rectangles on the wallpaper where pictures had hung for forty years. Sound behaves differently in an empty room. It stops pretending.

The piano stood in the front bay window — an upright, walnut veneer gone gray at the edges, one leg shimmed with a folded beer coaster. Carol, the daughter, stood beside it with her arms crossed in a way that suggested she'd been standing beside it for weeks, arguing with it.

"You can still take the check back," she said. "It's going to the church sale Saturday. I just wanted it tuned first. So it leaves in tune."

Vera set down her case. "That's a good reason."

"It's a stupid reason. Nobody at the church sale will know the difference."

"They'll know," Vera said. "They won't know they know."

Carol looked at her like she was deciding whether that was wisdom or nonsense, and then left the room, and Vera was grateful, because tuning was not a spectator sport.

She raised the lid. Dust, felt, brass. The smell came up out of the piano the way smell comes out of old books — wool and wood and time, a little sweetness underneath. She pulled the front panel and set it against the wall, and that was when she saw the pencil.

Someone had written on the wooden strip above the hammers, small letters in a careful hand, faded to the color of weak tea. Dates. Dozens of them, marching back in columns. *March 4. June 19. Sept 2.* And beside the dates, in the same hand, notes to herself:

*G# still sticky. Oiled it.*
*Thirds sound lazy. Practice slow.*
*A440. Finally.*

Fifty years of them. Vera crouched and read them all. A girl's handwriting at the top, rounded and earnest; an old woman's at the bottom, shakier, the letters leaning like tired guests. Between them, the same hand changing the way hands do, decade by decade, the way a river changes without ever being one river.

"Edith tuned it herself?" Vera called. "Or had it tuned?"

Carol came back to the doorway. "She tuned it herself. She was self-taught. Piano too, mostly. There was a book." A pause. "She never played for anyone. Not once that I saw. I'd hear it through the floor, and when I came down she'd be doing dishes."

Vera nodded. She'd heard this before, in one form or another — the player with no audience, the room above the kitchen. Forty years of tuning had taught her that most music is played to no one. The concert hall is the exception. The closed door is the rule.

She got to work. Muting wedges into the tenor, the strip of felt across the treble. She found the A above middle C and brought it to 440 with small, patient turns of the hammer — the pin doesn't want to move, then it moves too far, and the art is in the last quarter-turn, the one you make with your wrist and not your arm. Then octaves, stretched the way a piano wants to be stretched, not the way physics says. Then unisons, string by string, until each note was one voice and not three people talking.

The piano was in better shape than it had any right to be. Fresh strings in the treble — Edith had replaced them herself, judging by the knots, badly tied and holding anyway. The hammers were worn in the middle where the melody lives. Someone had played this piano the way some people pray: daily, privately, without expectation of answer.

Vera thought about the dates. March 4. June 19. Sept 2. Not holidays. Not birthdays. Ordinary days, chosen at random, or chosen for no reason at all — which is its own kind of devotion. You don't tune a piano for a recital you'll never give. You tune it because the sound of it matters to you, and to no one, and because the alternative is letting it drift, and you have decided — without ever saying it aloud — that some things should not be allowed to drift.

By the time she finished, the light had gone long and gold across the bare floor. She played a scale, then an arpeggio, then, because it seemed owed, a simple hymn — "Be Thou My Vision," the only one she could play without the book. In the empty room it sounded enormous. It sounded like the room had been waiting fifty years to be an auditorium.

When she turned around, Carol was in the doorway again, and she was crying the way people cry when they've been holding it at a specific angle for months and something finally knocked it loose.

"That's —" she started, and stopped. "Through the floor. That's what it was. All those years, that's what it was."

"Yes," Vera said.

"She was good."

"She was in tune," Vera said. "Mostly. The G sharp stuck until 1987."

Carol laughed, wet and surprised. "You read the —"

"I read everything. It's a diary," Vera said, closing the panel over it gently, the way you'd pull a blanket over someone sleeping. "The most honest one I've ever opened. Nobody writes in a piano for an audience."

She packed her tools, took the check, and at the door she turned back. The piano stood in the gold light, in tune, in an empty room, and it looked less like furniture than like a held breath.

"Whoever buys it Saturday," Vera said, "they'll never know what's written inside. But they'll know the piano's telling them the truth. It's the only thing it knows how to do."

Outside, the evening had that cool clarity that comes after a warm day. Vera got into her car and sat for a moment before starting it. Forty years, and the job still did this to her sometimes. Somewhere behind her, in a house with no furniture and no Edith, an A was holding steady at 440, faithful to a woman who had never once played for anyone, and who had, all along, been playing for the piano itself.
